TUESDAY, JUNE 9, 1925.
COMMERCE AND
HALL & HOLTZ
HANGHAI FIRM'S POSITION.

The interest taken in the meeting of Hall & Holtz, Ltd., is evidenced by the fact that just under twenty thousand shares out of a total of 26,000 shares were represented by those in attendance, and it may be stated in this connection that the list of shareholders in this company is a very extended one.

The balance sheet presented to the meeting, signed by Mr. E Barraclough, secretary and accountant, and Messrs. Seth Mancell and McLure, auditors, showed a debit balance at profit and loss of $8,781.32, debentures outstanding of something under three hundred thousand dollars, and over half a million due to the Hongkong & Shanghai Bank. On the asset side land and buildings were listed at over eight hundred thousand dollars and stock in hand was listed at more than six hundred thousand. The sundry debtors account stands at over a hundred thousand.
The following are the main points in the address to the assembled shareholders made by the Chairman, Mr. L. W. Hutton:

The turnover on the year's working, notwithstanding, a discount of $10 per cent. for cash purchases and a discount of 10% to shareholders was increased by over $88,000—whilst the overdraft which last year stood at $740,902 stood at $563,254 at the end of the year. Leaving out the amount realised by the sale of the Soochow Road property this meant a reduction during the past year of $82,643. The overdraft to day stood at $481,685, showing a still further reduction. The directors consider this is highly satisfactory, especially as during the past three months such reduction had been the result of purely normal trading, without resort to cheap sales or the sacrificing of stock. This reduction in overdraft meant a considerable saving in bank interest.
INCREASED TURNOVER.

Expense account showed a decrease of $18,500,—sundry creditors showed a small increase, but bills payable showed a decrease of over $5,000, and yet were substantially represented by goods in transit, (over $10,000).

All ascertainable liabilities had been taken into consideration in the accounts. Depreciation had been amply provided for, on all permanent assets, that on buildings having been written off against Property Reserve. Doubtless due to the 10% being allowed off cash purchases, Sundry debtors showed a substantial reduction, nearly $27,000 as compared with last year. With regard to stock on hand, this showed a decrease of close upon $100,000, and at least so far as the head office is concerned, stocks were clean and represented a fair value.

Considerable difficulty was experienced with the bakery department during the year but by alterations in the staff, a great saving in cost of production had been made. At the end of January, upon expiration of his agreement, the secretary Mr. G. H. Bartlett tendered his resignation, which had been accepted with regret, Mr. Barraclough, the accountant, had been appointed to the dual position of secretary and accountant, which appointment meant a saving to the company financially. More efficient service was obtained through combining the two positions.
MR. CUMINE'S CRITICISMS

Mr. H. M. Curnine in rather extended remarks, criticized the accounts from the point of view that they did not give the shareholders an idea of how the losses were being incurred—for instance was it worth while continuing the outport branches? As regards Shanghai, the Company had premises at the corner of the two busiest and most important thoroughfares in Shanghai, and yet the Company would not have been able to pay rent on the premises they occupy if they had to pay rent for them, instead of owning them.

Mr. Cumine then remarked that the statement of the profit and loss account showing a loss of $8,781.32 did not disclose the real situation. For one thing, the credit balance of last year of $7,894.02 had disappeared. Therefore, that meant that it had to be included in the losses. As regards the book value of the land, this had been raised by $263,690.63, taking advantage of the figures in the recent reassessment. Practically this same amount had been set down as a general reserve fund and from this $100,401.63 had been deducted as an amount written off stock, although the then Chairman at the meeting last year had stated that the value of the stock in hand was considerably below cost. This was a matter, said Mr. Cumine, which required further explanation. The actual loss for the year, Mr. Cumine contended, was really $117,077.87.

This is more than 20 per cent of our capital," exclaimed Mr. Cumine. "We cannot afford to allow this to continue. We have not been earning anything for many years. Our capital is dead to us. It is high time to save the founding ship."

Mr. Moller, the Chairman last year, said he agreed with some of Mr. Cumine's remarks, but he was not in favor of a suggestion made by Mr. Cumine that a committee of investigation should be appointed. He felt sure that the directors would only be too glad to give any shareholder every facility to inspect the accounts and would welcome suggestions.
Mr. Hutton remarked that that was certainly the case.

Mr. Cumine then proposed a resolution that the accounts be not accepted, and the meeting to be adjourned, the eventual idea being to convene an extraordinary meeting at which a committee of three or five shareholders to investigate the accounts and take suggestions should be appointed. As previously mentioned this was lost on a show of hands and also on a poll.
The accounts were then formally passed, Mr. W.S. King was re-elected a director, and Messrs. Seth, Mancel and Mc-Eure were appointed additors.
The Chairman in ringing the meeting to a close citerated that directors were always glad to give facilities to shareholders to inspect the accounts and invited suggestions.
ILOLO. TRADE.

APRIL'S INTERESTING
RETURNS

The aggregate value of native products imported into the port of Iloilo during the month of April last amounted to P9,254,429, while those exported to foreign countries reached a total value of P10,459,011 and the shipments to other domestic ports ran up to P92,925, according to a report of the agent of the Bureau of Commerce and Industry at that southern port.

The products imported into that port consisted of the following.
From Occidental Negros: 38,021,906 kilos of centrifugal sugar valued at P6,843,943; 3,896,028 kilos of muscovado costing P701,285; 1,378,020 board feet of lumber to the value of P123,572; 183,752 kilos of sundried copra at a cost of P32,945; 110,360 kilos of alcohol valued at P28,715; and P11,695 worth of other products; from other parts of Pannay Island: 6,194,582 kilos of muscovado sugar costing P743,349; 1,306,420 kilos of centrifugal sugar to the value of P235,155; 383,644 kilos of sundried copra at a cost of P82,189; 42,289,425 kilos of abacab� value at P32,624; 673 kilos of knorted pina fibre costing P33,581; 205,036 kilos of fertilizer to the value of P24,600; 1,673,306 kilos of palay at a cost of P21,287; 354,000 pieces of firewood valued at P17,340; 298,800 bayones costing P14,340; P4,922 worth of other products; from Manila: 1,156,316 kilos rice to the value of P191,637; 157,000 kilos of fertilizer at a cost of P14,440; 170,922 kilos of salt valued at P5,383; 6,120 kilos of leaf tobacco costing P5,175; 2,507 railroad ties to the value of P5,014; 13,871 kilos of mango at a cost of P1,000; from Cebu: 96,919 kilos of sundried copra valued at P19,220; 16,707 kilos of leaf tobacco costing P12,500; 165,627 kilos of muscovado sugar to the value of P10,979; and P642 worth of other products.

In a letter to the “Times” on the question of the nationalisation of banking, which is again being urged in certain quarters, Mr. Walter Runciman gave figures showing how widely banking shares are held by investors in Britain. The paid-up capital of the “Big Five” English banks is £60½ million, and there are no less than 275,400 shareholders, giving an average no-final shareholding of only £219 5s. These figures are a strong argument against the agitation for handing over the business of banking in Britain to the State. The revival of the discussion of this topic has had no effect whatever upon the market prices of banking shares, which during the recent uncertainty in markets have remained remarkably steady. The shares of the Midland Bank, for example, stand at a figure which gives a yield of just under 5 per cent., and although this is a special case, since rights attach to the shares for subscription to a new issue below market price, the quotations for the shares of the four other large banks are such that the yields obtainable are relatively low. Possibly the reason is that higher dividends are anticipated for the current year. It is certainly highly improbable that dividends will be reduced, and if the volume of loans and advances continues to expand at its present rate and conditions in the money market remain favourable, an expansion in banking profits will no doubt be shown at the end of the year.
BANK SHARES.
WEEKS AND CO.

Speaking at the meeting of Weeks and Co., Ltd., the Chairman, Mr. T. E. Trudman expressed regret that the year's working had again resulted in loss. Conditions of trade similar to those in the preceding year had again prevailed, and while the gross gain on the turnover was practically the same, they had to reduce selling prices in many instances to a very low margin to move the stock. Added to this, they had to face the writing down of a lot of stock in the Hankow branch which had been accumulated by the recent manager. The cause for writing down was not that the stocks has deteriorated or was in any way bad; in the contrary the bulk was of excellent quality and in perfect condition, but it had to be brought down to present day valuation and below, in order to enable the company to reduce the quantity to a normal figure. The action thus taken would place the Hankow branch in a position to sell at keenly cut prices. In Shanghai stocks are in excellent condition and stood at present day market value.

The trade working expenses, Mr. Trueman explained, were less than for the preceding year due in the main to the smaller charge for interest, by the gradual reduction of the overdraft—a satisfactory feature. Interest charges were a heavy item and this was due of course to the fact that the trading capital had only been increased by $36,410 since 1903, (the other $200,000 having been used entirely in the purchase of their property), while the turnover had increased by 150 per cent. and the stock had increased proportionately. This meant that interest was being paid to the Bank instead of dividends to the shareholders as would have been the case if the company had adequate capital.

All assets, said Mr. Trueman, appear in the balance sheet at much below their intrinsic or market value.
The Bank overdraft was $33,705.67 less than last year and $93,778.04 less than the combined overdraft and debentures in 1923, while sundry creditors stood at $1,185.18 more.

Mr. Trueman then referred to a letter from a Shareholder which asked the directors to give the shareholders some indication as to the future prospects of the company. "Shareholders need have no fear as to the financial stability of the company," said Mr. Trueman. "From the balance sheet you will see stocks in Shanghai and Hankow more than balance the bank overdraft while assessed value of the land without buildings more than covers the share issue by almost a lack of dollars."
The 1924 assessed value of the Shanghai land was nearly Tls. 120,000.00 (Tls: 119,785.66) more than book value of the land building.
POOR DIVIDEND PROSPECTS

The disconcerting part is the fact that we have paid no dividends for the past two years. This apart from trade depression is in fact due, as I have already mentioned, to interest going to the Bank in lieu of to shareholders, due to our inadequate capital. To reduce the capital of a Company, is a relatively easy matter, but to increase our capital at the present time is not so. We have had this matter under consideration for some time and this is all I can say at present to you. With regard to future prospects I think I can quite safely say that you will not receive next year such a bad report, but until trade revived and the public are spending money more freely, added to our lack of capital already referred to, the prospects of a dividend are not too good.
The accounts were favourably passed.

For the year to the end of November last the Warrington soap company of Joseph Crosfield and Sons—all the ordinary shares in which are held by Lever Bros.—made a profit of £384,063, against £331,269 earned in the previous year, and £330,937 in the year to November 30, 1922. This figure is arrived at, after charging for repairs, renewals, and alterations, depreciation and insurance. No change is made in the ordinary dividend, which has been at the rate of 10 per cent since 1922, the whole of the increased profit being added to the amount carried forward, raising it to £56,564, against the £3,768 so dealt with a year ago. The dividend on the ordinary share was formerly "not divulged to the public," but after the issue of £1,500,000 7½ per cent cumulative A preference shares in March, 1920, it was announced, when the results for that year were made known, that the dividend on the ordinary shares would be at the rate of 12½ per cent.
